candidate_sources.title: Cercospora longipes (brown leaf spot of sugarcane) | CABI Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: The official CABI Compendium datasheet for Cercospora longipes (brown leaf spot of sugarcane) covers Identity, Distribution, Hosts/Species Affected, symptoms, biology, epidemiology, and management. C. longipes has a restricted host range with only Saccharum officinarum (sugarcane), S. spontaneum, S. robustum and Sorghum vulgare being infected.

candidate_sources.title: Brown spot of sugarcane: an emerging disease in South Western region in India
candidate_sources.snippet: Brown spot of sugarcane caused by Cercospora longipes is an emerging disease documented with severe outbreaks in parts of Karnataka and Maharashtra. Brown spot causes a loss in cane yield of at least 14% and results in a loss up to 18% in terms of sugar production. Conidiophore fascicles emerge near the stomatal pores (50-200μm diameter, ~50-250μm height). Spore germination is favored by light and high relative humidity above 95%.

candidate_sources.title: Brown spot disease of sugarcane caused by Cercospora longipes (Butler) | RUFORUM Institutional Repository
candidate_sources.snippet: Research on biology, epidemiology and control of brown spot disease of sugarcane caused by Cercospora longipes. Spraying once a month at the rate of 2.50 kg/ha of Dithane M 45 in 900 litres was the best for controlling the disease. No variety was found immune; tolerant varieties include B 3172 and M 423-51, while CP 29/305 and PR 975 are highly susceptible.

candidate_sources.title: Diseases of Sugarcane — Disease group, Name of the disease, Causal organism
candidate_sources.snippet: University teaching document covering diseases of sugarcane including brown spot caused by Cercospora longipes along with symptoms and causal organism details for major fungal and bacterial diseases of sugarcane.

candidate_sources.title: Sugarcane Diseases: Gummosis and Leaf Scald | Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service
candidate_sources.snippet: Leaf scald is a vascular disease caused by the bacterium Xanthomonas albilineans, characterized by creamy or grayish streaking and later withering of the leaves. Gummosis: mature leaves develop longitudinal stripes which initially appear pale yellow and later turn brown, with affected tissues slowly drying up.

candidate_sources.title: Integrated Disease Management of Sugarcane
candidate_sources.snippet: Bands of dead tissue develop along pencil lines starting at the leaf margin and may expand until the entire leaf is dead; young shoots may be killed; and under severe disease conditions, entire plants may die. Varietal resistance is the best means of control.

candidate_sources.title: Present Status and Future Management Strategies for Sugarcane Yellow Leaf Virus: A Major Constraint to the Global Sugarcane Production
candidate_sources.snippet: Complete drying of leaf foliage with stunted and poor growth was observed due to severe incidence of the disease under field situations. Necrosis is observed from tip to the base of leaves, and the spindle dries along with the leaves.

candidate_sources.title: Sugarcane | Texas Plant Disease Handbook
candidate_sources.snippet: Comprehensive guide to sugarcane diseases including leaf scald, red rot, yellow leaf, and gummosis. Symptoms include yellowing, withering, and drying of leaves with associated pathogen identification and management practices.

candidate_sources.title: SSAGR203/SC003: Sugarcane Eyespot Disease
candidate_sources.snippet: Sugarcane Eyespot Disease — UF/IFAS EDIS extension factsheet. First observable symptoms are minute water-soaked spots on young leaves. Typical mature eyespot symptoms are reddish-brown elliptical lesions (0.5–4.0 mm long) with yellowish-brown margins, and reddish-brown 'runner' streaks extending toward the leaf tip. Caused by the fungus Bipolaris sacchari. Control is by resistant clones; fungicides are not practical.

candidate_sources.title: Bipolaris sacchari (eye spot) | CABI Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: CABI Compendium datasheet on Bipolaris sacchari (eye spot of sugarcane). Covers Identity, Overview, Distribution, Dispersal, Hosts/Species Affected, Diagnosis, Biology & Ecology, Seedborne Aspects, Impacts, Prevention/Control. Previous names include Cercospora sacchari, Drechslera sacchari and Helminthosporium sacchari. Produces host-specific helminthosporoside toxins.

candidate_sources.title: Fact sheet - Sugarcane eye spot (305)
candidate_sources.snippet: Pacific Pests, Pathogens & Weeds factsheet dedicated to sugarcane eye spot. Describes water-soaked lesions, reddish-brown elliptical spots with yellow halos, and runner streaks on leaves caused by Bipolaris sacchari (Helminthosporium sacchari). Includes symptoms, spread by wind-borne conidia, favoring conditions, and management via resistant cultivars.

candidate_sources.title: Sugarcane grassy shoot phytoplasma (grassy shoot of sugarcane) | CABI Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: CABI datasheet covering Identity, Overview, Distribution, Dispersal, Hosts/Species Affected, Vectors & Intermediate Hosts, Diagnosis, Biology & Ecology, Environmental Requirements, Seedborne Aspects, Impacts, and Prevention/Control for Sugarcane grassy shoot phytoplasma.

candidate_sources.title: SUGARCANE :: MAJOR DISEASE :: GRASSY SHOOT
candidate_sources.snippet: Sugarcane Grassy Shoot lecture note: symptoms include profuse tillering with thin, chlorotic white/yellow leaves giving grassy appearance, stunted growth, reduced internodal length. Caused by phytoplasma; transmitted through setts and leafhopper vectors. Management via healthy seed, rogueing, and moist hot air treatment.

candidate_sources.title: Grassy Shoot Disease on Sugarcane Management
candidate_sources.snippet: Vasantdada Sugar Institute factsheet on Grassy Shoot Disease (GSD) of sugarcane. Discusses causal phytoplasma ('Candidatus Phytoplasma sacchari'), typical symptoms of proliferous tillering and chlorotic grass-like leaves, spread via infected setts and leafhopper vectors, and integrated management including heat therapy, tissue-culture seed, and rogueing.

candidate_sources.title: Sugarcane Grassy Shoot (SCGS) Disease - An Overview
candidate_sources.snippet: Peer-reviewed review article on Sugarcane Grassy Shoot (SCGS) disease associated with 'Candidatus Phytoplasma sacchari'. Covers symptomatology (chlorotic thin leaves, profuse tillering, stunted growth), detection (PCR/nested PCR), epidemiology, vectors (Deltocephalus vulgaris and other leafhoppers), yield losses up to 100%, and management practices.

candidate_sources.title: Sugarcane Pokkah Boeng Disease: Insights and Future Directions for Effective Management
candidate_sources.snippet: Pokkah Boeng disease has been observed in nearly all countries where sugarcane is commercially cultivated and is caused by fungi, specifically the Fusarium fungal complex. Fusarium fujikuroi, F. sacchari, F. oxysporum, F. verticillioides, F. proliferatum, and F. subglutinans are the major species causing the disease. Primarily airborne, secondary transmission via infected setts, irrigation water, splashed rain, and soil. Management: resistant varieties, removal of top rot/knife cut canes, 0.1% carbendazim, 0.2% copper oxychloride, or 0.3% mancozeb sprays at 15-day intervals.

candidate_sources.title: Identification and Characterization of Pathogenic and Endophytic Fungal Species Associated with Pokkah Boeng Disease of Sugarcane
candidate_sources.snippet: Pokkah Boeng disease symptoms include red streaking and chlorosis, stalk rot, and knife cut with deformed top. Five Fusarium species have been identified as causal agents: F. incarnatum, F. andiyazi, F. sacchari, F. proliferatum, and F. verticillioides. The fungus Fusarium verticillioides (formerly Fusarium moniliforme) is an Ascomycete fungus of the order Hypocreales, family Nectriaceae.

candidate_sources.title: Pokkah Boeng Causal organism - Vasantdada Sugar Institute
candidate_sources.snippet: Pokkah Boeng causal organism factsheet covering symptoms (chlorotic phase, top rot phase, knife cut phase), pathogen (Fusarium moniliforme / F. verticillioides), disease cycle and management recommendations for sugarcane growers.

candidate_sources.title: Pokkah Boeng | Pests & Diseases - Plantix
candidate_sources.snippet: Symptoms include chlorotic phase, top rot phase, knife cut phase, ladder-like lesions on shoot, twisted leaves, and malformed shoot. The disease is caused by Fusarium moniliforme and typically emerges during hot and humid conditions. Management includes resistant varieties, removal of infected canes, and fungicide sprays.

candidate_sources.title: First Report of Bipolaris bicolor Causing Red Spot on Sugarcane in Guangdong
candidate_sources.snippet: First Report of Bipolaris bicolor Causing Red Spot on Sugarcane in Guangdong — APS Plant Disease publication documenting a new pathogen causing red spot lesions on sugarcane leaves, with pathogen identification, symptomatology, and pathogenicity tests.

candidate_sources.title: Diseases of Sugarcane — PATH 272 Lecture 6/7 (TNAU eAgri)
candidate_sources.snippet: Lecture covering diseases of sugarcane including red rot, red spot / red leaf spot (Dimeriella sacchari), ring spot, rust, smut, wilt, and grassy shoot, with symptoms, causal organisms, disease cycle, and management practices.

candidate_sources.title: List of sugarcane diseases — Wikipedia
candidate_sources.snippet: Comprehensive list of sugarcane diseases and their causal organisms, including red spot / red leaf spot (Dimeriella sacchari; synonyms include Leptosphaeria sacchari and Mycovellosiella), red rot (Colletotrichum falcatum), ring spot, and others.

candidate_sources.title: SUGARCANE :: MAJOR DISEASE :: SETT ROT OR PINEAPPLE DISEASE
candidate_sources.snippet: Affected tissues first develop a reddish colour which turns to brownish black in the later stages. Yellowish stripes develop at growing points of the shoot which later turn reddish brown; rotting may commence from the tip of the shoot and spreads downwards. Setts treated with hot water at 52°C for 18 minutes render good control of the disease.

candidate_sources.title: Sugarcane pineapple disease (218) - Lucid Apps (Pacific Pests, Pathogens & Weeds)
candidate_sources.snippet: Pineapple sett rot, caused by Ceratocystis paradoxa, is an economically important disease of sugarcane worldwide. The fungus enters cut ends, turning tissues red and then black with a pineapple smell. Buds and roots fail, plants dieback or are stunted with low sugar content. Control by hot water treatment of setts and fungicides.

candidate_sources.title: Ceratocystis paradoxa (black rot of pineapple) | CABI Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: CABI datasheet on Ceratocystis paradoxa, the causal agent of pineapple sett rot of sugarcane, describing host range, symptoms (reddish to black internal discoloration, pineapple odor), distribution, biology, and management including hot water sett treatment and fungicidal dips.

candidate_sources.title: Surveying Potential Soilborne Pathogens Causing Sett Rot on Sugarcane in Southern Florida | Plant Disease
candidate_sources.snippet: APS Plant Disease publication surveying soilborne pathogens associated with sett rot on sugarcane in southern Florida, identifying Thielaviopsis/Ceratocystis paradoxa and related fungi, with symptom descriptions and pathogenicity assessments.

candidate_sources.title: Sugarcane Smut, Caused by Sporisorium scitamineum, a Major Disease of Sugarcane: A Contemporary Review | Phytopathology
candidate_sources.snippet: Sugarcane smut caused by the fungus Sporisorium scitamineum is one of the major diseases of sugarcane worldwide, causing significant losses in productivity and profitability. The disease is easily recognized by its long whiplike sorus produced on the apex or side shoots of sugarcane stalks. Teliospores are airborne, can travel long distances, and remain viable in hot and dry conditions for >6 months. The most effective method of managing this disease is via resistant varieties.

candidate_sources.title: Sporisorium scitamineum (sugarcane smut) - CABI Compendium Datasheet
candidate_sources.snippet: CABI Compendium datasheet on Sporisorium scitamineum (sugarcane smut), including pathogen identity, host range, distribution, symptoms (whip-like sori at stalk apices, chlorotic and elongated leaves, increased tillering), biology, epidemiology, and management.

candidate_sources.title: Sugarcane Smut: Current Knowledge and the Way Forward for Management - PMC
candidate_sources.snippet: Comprehensive review of sugarcane smut (Sporisorium scitamineum): symptoms including whip-like sori, leaf and stem galls and bud proliferation; airborne teliospore dispersal (up to 100 million spores per sorus per day); spread via systemically infested planting material; integrated management combining resistant cultivars, healthy planting material, and crop rotation.
